arml-1999-power-01a.prompt:
*(Power Question 1999: Judgment Day.)* A **permutation** of $S=\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ is a one-to-one function $p$ from $S$ onto $S$, written as the list of its values $p(1)\,p(2)\cdots p(n)$; for example $p=2\,4\,1\,3$ means $p(1)=2$, $p(2)=4$, $p(3)=1$, $p(4)=3$. A **pair** is an ordered pair $(j,k)$ with $j<k$ (so $(3,5)$ is a pair but $(5,3)$ is not). The **turnabout set** $T(p)$ of a permutation $p$ is the set of pairs $(j,k)$ with $p(j)>p(k)$, and the **turnabout number** $N(p)$ is the number of pairs in $T(p)$. For example, $p=3\,2\,5\,4\,1$ has $T(p)=\{(1,2),(1,5),(2,5),(3,4),(3,5),(4,5)\}$ and $N(p)=6$.

Find the turnabout set $T$ and the turnabout number $N$ of the permutation $1\,2\,3\,4\,5\,6$.

*(Power Question 1999: Judgment Day, Part II.)* Recall: a permutation $p$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is a list $p(1)\cdots p(n)$ of its values; a pair is $(j,k)$ with $j<k$; the turnabout set $T(p)$ is the set of pairs with $p(j)>p(k)$ and $N(p)$ is its size. Given permutations $p_1,\dots,p_m$, their **functional sum** $P=p_1+\dots+p_m$ is the function $P(x)=p_1(x)+\dots+p_m(x)$; for example $p_1=5\,4\,3\,1\,2$, $p_2=4\,2\,3\,1\,5$, $p_3=2\,3\,1\,4\,5$ give $P=11\,9\,7\,6\,12$. (Motivation: three judges rank $4$ skaters; for each pair of skaters you agree with exactly two judges; the sum of the judges' rankings gives the same order as yours.)

arml-1999-power-10.prompt:
*(Power Question 1999: Judgment Day, Part II.)* Recall: a permutation $p$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is a list $p(1)\cdots p(n)$ of its values; a pair is $(j,k)$ with $j<k$; the turnabout set $T(p)$ is the set of pairs with $p(j)>p(k)$ and $N(p)$ is its size. (Motivation: three judges rank $4$ skaters; for each pair of skaters you agree with exactly two judges; the sum of the judges' rankings gives the same order as yours.)
